Transformational Familiarity:
Food Neophobia, Autonomy, and the Construction of Taste


                                    Flyxion
                                 Independent Researcher

                               October 2026



                                           Abstract

     Children who refuse unfamiliar foods are usually described as picky, a label that treats
     a heterogeneous set of behaviors as a single defect to be corrected. This essay argues
      that the label obscures at least ﬁve distinct processes: neophobia toward novelty, sensory
      aversion to particular properties, a stable preference for familiar foods, ordinary variation
      in appetite, and resistance to coercion. These produce similar behavior at the table but call
      for different responses, and some of them are made worse by the interventions that work
       for others. Drawing on the literature on exposure, social modeling, responsive feeding, and
     food categorization, the essay develops a framework in which acceptance of a food depends
     on how that food is connected to the child’s existing categories and on how much control
      the child retains over the pace of approach. It proposes the Transformational Familiarity
      Hypothesis: under safe, voluntary, and pace-controlled conditions, an unfamiliar food
     becomes more approachable when it is introduced through a sequence of preparations that
      preserve recognizable features of an already accepted food. The hypothesis is formalized,
      distinguished from the established ﬁndings on repeated exposure, and paired with a
     worked example, a typology of sensory, procedural, and causal familiarity, and a protocol
     by which it could be tested. Its conclusion is that food acceptance depends in part on the
      ﬂexibility of the surrounding food environment, and not solely on the ﬂexibility of the
       eater.

1  Introduction


Few childhood behaviors generate as much household conﬂict, and as little agreement about
cause, as the refusal of food. Parents, clinicians, and grandparents hold conﬁdent and mutually
incompatible views about what picky eating is and what should be done about it. Some regard
it as a discipline problem to be settled by ﬁrmness, others as a temperament to be waited out,
others as a sensory difference that must be accommodated, and others as a symptom that the
child has been given too many alternatives. Each of these views is supported by cases in which
it appears to have worked, and each fails in cases that the others handle easily. A framework
that accounts for this pattern of partial success is more useful than another prescription.

   The central claim of this essay is that picky eating is best understood as a problem about
how foods are introduced, classiﬁed, and made available for exploration, and only secondarily
as a property of the child. A refusal is a response to a particular food, in a particular form,
presented under particular conditions, and each of those three elements can be altered by
the adults who organize the meal. This does not deny that children differ in temperament,
sensory sensitivity, and the strength of their neophobia. A twin study of children aged 8
to 11 estimated the heritability of food neophobia at 0.78 (Cooke et al., 2007). Heritability
describes the share of variation in a trait that is attributable to genetic differences within a
particular population and environment. It does not mean that 78 percent of any individual
child’s neophobia is genetically determined, and it does not set a limit on the inﬂuence that
changes in the environment can have. Some children also have feeding difﬁculties of clinical
signiﬁcance. The claim is that, within the range of ordinary variation, the structure of the food
environment contributes to the outcome, and that this contribution is both larger and more
tractable than the vocabulary of defect and discipline suggests.

   The contribution of the essay can be located precisely. The repeated-exposure literature is
concerned with changing the eater’s response to a ﬁxed food, by presenting the same item until
it becomes familiar. The proposal developed here is concerned with changing the pathway
by which the eater encounters the food, and treats the history of encounters, together with
the form of the food and the child’s state, as what determines the response. The ﬁrst is a
well-supported account of one mechanism. The second is a conjecture about a different and
possibly complementary mechanism, and separating it from the ﬁrst is the main burden of the
formal development and the experimental protocol.

   The essay proceeds in four movements. The ﬁrst (Sections 2 and 3) separates the phenom-
ena that are grouped under the picky-eating label and reviews what the empirical literature
establishes about exposure, modeling, and pressure. The second (Sections 4 and 5) develops a
theory of food categories and proposes the Transformational Familiarity Hypothesis, a conjec-
ture about the use of intermediate preparations to connect accepted and unaccepted foods. The
third (Sections 6 through 9) examines the conditions under which such transformations are
likely to work: observational and participatory involvement, procedural and causal familiarity
gained through cultivation and cooking, a distribution of agency in which adults structure the
environment and children retain authority over participation, and the culinary competence
that makes a ﬂexible environment affordable. The fourth (Sections 10 through 12) states the

limits of the argument, proposes an experimental protocol, and concludes.

  A note on status is necessary at the outset. The established literature on repeated exposure
and social modeling is substantial and is reviewed here as such. The central hypothesis
of the essay, by contrast, is a proposal, not a ﬁnding. Observations from ordinary cooking
suggest that foods connected by overlapping properties are easier to approach than foods
presented without such connections, but observations of this kind are vulnerable to every
familiar confound: the child may have simply grown older, the adult may have simply become
more skilled, and repeated exposure may have done the work attributed to the transformation.
The purpose of the formal apparatus developed below is to make the proposal precise enough
that it can fail.


2  Picky Eating Is Not a Unitary Phenomenon


The terms picky eating, fussy eating, and food fussiness are used in the research literature and
in everyday speech with considerable looseness. Dovey et al. (2008) reviewed the ﬁeld and
distinguished food neophobia, the reluctance to eat new foods, from picky or fussy eating,
which involves rejecting a substantial range of foods that are familiar as well as unfamiliar,
while noting that the two constructs are inter-related and share some inﬂuences. Behaviors that
look alike at the table therefore need not share a cause, and the labels are applied inconsistently
in everyday speech. The ﬁrst task of any serious account is therefore to disaggregate the
category.

   Five distinct processes can be separated analytically, with the understanding that they
overlap in practice. The ﬁrst is food neophobia, the reluctance to eat or try novel foods, which has
been measured in adults with an established scale (Pliner and Hobden, 1992) and in children
with parent-report and behavioral measures (Pliner, 1994). In an omnivore, neophobia is
understood as one side of a balance. An animal that eats many kinds of food needs to explore
unfamiliar items in order to meet its nutritional needs, and needs caution about them in order
to avoid ingesting toxins (Rozin, 1976). Neophobia is accordingly an adaptive disposition, and
its strength in early childhood coincides with the period in which children become mobile and
independent enough to ingest things their caregivers have not vetted.

   The second process is sensory aversion, a negative response to a speciﬁc property of a food,
such as a texture, a temperature, a bitterness, or a smell. This differs from neophobia because
it can attach to foods the child has encountered many times, and because it need not diminish
with exposure. Food selectivity is common in children with autism spectrum disorders, and
a narrative review discusses sensory sensitivity as a possible contributor to it (Cermak et al.,
2010). The distinction has practical weight. A child who rejects a novel food because it is novel
is likely to respond to repeated, low-pressure contact. A child who rejects a food because its
texture is aversive may not, and may be distressed by the repetition.

   The third process is a stable preference for familiar foods, which is distinct from neophobia in
that the child may be willing to taste something new but consistently prefers an established set.
Such a preference is not pathological. The set of accepted foods in early childhood is narrow in

most children and broadens with age, and an observer who measured only the breadth of the
repertoire at a single time would conﬂate a child who is still broadening with a child whose
repertoire has stalled.

   The fourth process is variation in appetite. Young children regulate their energy intake across
days more accurately than they do within any single meal, so that a refused meal is often
followed by a larger one. A behavior that appears as picky eating at one meal may be an
appropriate response to satiety from a snack or a growth-related ﬂuctuation in need. Treating
each refusal as informative about preference, without attending to appetite, produces false
positives.

   The ﬁfth process is resistance to coercion. Evidence from several designs suggests that
pressure to eat can run counter to its intended effect. Experimental work on restriction and
pressure indicates that making a food conditional or forbidden increases its salience and
desirability (Fisher and Birch, 1999). A longitudinal study of girls and their mothers found that
mothers who ate more fruit and vegetables used less pressure and had daughters who were
less picky and ate more fruit and vegetables (Galloway et al., 2005), which associates pressure
with pickiness without establishing whether pressure produces refusal, refusal elicits pressure,
or both arise from another variable. Retrospective studies of forced consumption episodes
ﬁnd that adults frequently report lasting aversions to foods that they were compelled to eat
as children (Batsell et al., 2002). Some portion of what presents as picky eating is therefore
produced by the mealtime dynamics that adults introduce in response to earlier refusals, a
feedback loop in which the remedy sustains the problem.

   Beyond these ﬁve lies a sixth category that differs in kind: clinically signiﬁcant feeding
disorders. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, as deﬁned in the ﬁfth edition of the
American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual, describes persistent failure to meet
nutritional needs associated with signiﬁcant weight loss, nutritional deﬁciency, dependence on
supplements, or psychosocial impairment, and is not explained by lack of food or by culturally
sanctioned practice (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Children in this category need
specialist assessment, and the techniques discussed in this essay are not a substitute for it. The
disaggregation matters most here, because the same behavior that is a developmental stage in
one child is a medical problem in another.

   The disaggregation also yields a practical consequence that recurs in the sections that
follow. Interventions are targeted at mechanisms, and a single outward behavior can have
any of several mechanisms behind it. Repeated low-pressure exposure addresses neophobia.
Textural accommodation addresses sensory aversion. Predictable meal structure and tolerance
of variable appetite address the fourth process. Withdrawal of pressure addresses the ﬁfth. A
caregiver who applies the intervention for one mechanism to a child whose behavior arises
from another will observe failure and may conclude that the child is intractable, when the
more accurate conclusion is that the diagnosis of the refusal was wrong.

3  What the Evidence Establishes: Exposure, Modeling, and Pressure


Before introducing a new hypothesis it is necessary to state what the literature supports, since
the hypothesis must be distinguished from it.


3.1  Repeated exposure

The most robust ﬁnding in the study of children’s food acceptance is that repeated tasting of a
novel food increases liking for and consumption of it. In an early experimental demonstration,
Birch and Marlin (1982) showed that two-year-old children’s preferences shifted toward
foods to which they had been exposed more often, an extension to food of the broader mere-
exposure effect described by Zajonc (1968). Subsequent work has replicated the pattern
across ages and foods, including with initially disliked vegetables in infants (Maier et al.,
2007) and with a vegetable that children initially disliked (Wardle et al., 2003). Cooke (2007)
reviewed laboratory and naturalistic studies and concluded that repeated opportunities to
taste unfamiliar foods increase liking and consumption, and that familiarity is perhaps the
most important determinant of a child’s liking for a food. The number of exposures needed
varies. In one study of infants, intake of an initially disliked vegetable rose to match that of a
liked one by the eighth exposure (Maier et al., 2007).

  Two qualiﬁcations are important for the argument developed here. The ﬁrst concerns
the kind of exposure. In a study of two- to ﬁve-year-olds that separated looking exposure
from tasting exposure to novel fruits, Birch et al. (1987) found that looking raised visual
preference judgments but did not raise taste preference judgments for foods that were never
tasted, whereas tasting raised both, and concluded that experience must engage the modality
relevant to the judgment. The result cautions against the assumption that familiarity with the
appearance of a food converts into willingness to eat it. Later work complicates the picture.
Picture books depicting foods increased toddlers’ visual preferences for the pictured items,
and for new pictures of them (Houston-Price et al., 2009), and a nursery intervention in which
children aged 12 to 36 months looked at, listened to, felt, and smelled unusual fruits and
vegetables for four weeks increased their touching and tasting of those foods at a later meal,
compared with a control group (Dazeley and Houston-Price, 2015). Enjoyment of tactile
play has also been associated with lower food neophobia in preschool children (Coulthard
and Thakker, 2015), though this association is correlational. The overall pattern is that non-
taste exposure may help, that its effects are less consistent than those of tasting, and that the
conditions under which it helps are not fully characterized.

   The second qualiﬁcation is that exposure is generally studied for a single food presented
repeatedly in a ﬁxed form. The literature has less to say about what happens when the form
of the food is varied across exposures, or when acceptance of one food generalizes to related
foods. There is some evidence of generalization. In a sample of infants aged four to seven
months who were fed a target food daily for ten days, Birch et al. (1998) found that intake of
the target rose, that intake of the same food from another manufacturer and of similar foods
also rose, and that intake of a different food did not change. This suggests that acceptance is

partly organized by similarity and does not attach only to the speciﬁc item, though the sample
was small, the infants were young, and the authors note that infants may have difﬁculty
discriminating among many foods. This ﬁnding is the empirical foothold for the argument of
Section 5, since it implies that the structure of similarity among foods matters to what children
accept.

  A third qualiﬁcation concerns outcomes. Studies of exposure report increases in liking,
in willingness to taste, and in intake, and these are related but not interchangeable. A child
may consume a food more readily without rating it as more pleasant, and may rate it as more
pleasant without eating more of it. Claims about the effectiveness of exposure should be read at
the level at which the outcome was measured, and the same caution applies to the hypotheses
developed below.


3.2  Social modeling

A second well-supported ﬁnding is that children’s acceptance of foods is inﬂuenced by watch-
ing others eat. Early experimental work reported that an adult eating an unfamiliar food
increased young children’s willingness to taste it (Harper and Sanders, 1975). The manner of
modeling matters. In a series of preschool quasi-experiments, silent teacher modeling did not
encourage acceptance, whereas enthusiastic modeling maintained acceptance of a new food
across ﬁve meals, and the addition of a competing peer model removed the effect (Hendy and
Raudenbush, 2000). A school-based program combining peer modeling, reward, and repeated
exposure reduced neophobia in children (Laureati et al., 2014). The theoretical background is
the social learning framework of Bandura (1977), according to which behavior is acquired in
part through observation of models who are similar, competent, or valued.

   The evidence for modeling is respectable but is not uniform, and several features limit its
application. The effect of modeling depends on its manner, as the preschool studies above show,
and in one of them acceptance of a new food was greatest at the ﬁrst meal and then dropped.
Moreover, modeling interacts with pressure. An adult who eats a food while simultaneously
urging a child to eat it provides two signals, one of which may undermine the other. For
present purposes the relevant point is that observation of a trusted person eating a food is a
plausible route by which children come to regard the food as safe, and that this route does
not require the child to eat anything at the moment of observation. The evidence on manner
suggests that modeling is more effective when it is enthusiastic than when it is silent, which is
a different thing from pressure.


3.3  Pressure and restriction

The third body of evidence, reviewed in Section 2, concerns the effects of coercion. The
available evidence suggests that the direction of the effect is not merely neutral, although the
designs differ in strength. Retrospective reports link forced consumption to lasting rejection
of the food (Batsell et al., 2002), and longitudinal data link maternal pressure to picky eating
in daughters (Galloway et al., 2005). Neither design establishes causation, and the review of

Dovey et al. (2008) lists pressure to eat among the factors that inﬂuence both neophobia and
picky eating. Restricting access to appealing foods similarly increases the child’s attention to
and desire for them (Fisher and Birch, 1999). The practical lesson, which converges with the
clinical responsive-feeding literature (Black and Aboud, 2011), is that how a food is offered
affects the response to it, independently of the food itself.


3.4  What remains unexplained

These three bodies of evidence together describe a set of effective conditions: repeated, pressure-
free contact, accompanied by the example of a trusted eater. They leave open at least three
questions that bear on the remainder of this essay. First, why does exposure sometimes fail,
and what can be done in those cases other than to persist? Second, how does acceptance spread
among foods, so that the work done on one food reduces the work required for another? Third,
what role is played by the child’s own control over the process, as opposed to the mere absence
of pressure? The hypothesis that follows is an attempt to give a structured answer to the ﬁrst
two, and the discussion of agency in Section 8 addresses the third.


4  Food Categories and the Structure of Familiarity


Sections 3 to 5 form the spine of the argument. The preceding section established what
exposure and modeling can and cannot explain, this section supplies the account of food
categories on which the hypothesis depends, and the next section states the hypothesis.

  A food is never encountered as a bare collection of sensory properties. It is encountered
as a member of a category, and the category determines what is expected of it. A child who
has learned that crackers are crisp, savory, and dry has a set of expectations that is violated
by a soft cracker, and the violation may be experienced as a reason for rejection even when
the soft cracker would be perfectly acceptable if presented as something else. Understanding
picky eating therefore requires a theory of how children structure food categories and how the
boundaries of those categories are drawn.


4.1  Prototypes and family resemblance

The psychology of categorization offers two relevant ideas. The ﬁrst is that natural categories
are organized around prototypes, with membership graded by similarity to a central exemplar,
and not deﬁned by necessary and sufﬁcient conditions (Rosch and Mervis, 1975). The second,
which precedes the psychological work, is the philosophical observation by Wittgenstein (1953)
that many concepts are held together by overlapping similarities, a family resemblance, and
not by a single shared feature. Applied to food, these ideas suggest that a child’s category of,
say, pizza is not a rule but a cluster. A prototypical pizza may have a round shape, a baked
crust, tomato sauce, and melted cheese, and an item that shares several of these properties is a
better or worse member of the category according to how many it shares.


                                         9

If this is correct, then the boundaries of a food category are soft, and the child’s willingness
to accept a novel item depends on how well it ﬁts into a category that is already accepted. This
explains some familiar observations. A child who rejects a vegetable served alone may accept
it as a topping on a food from an accepted category, and a child who rejects a homemade
version of a familiar item may be responding to the failure of the homemade version to match
the prototype, such as a differently shaped nugget or an unfamiliar brand of crackers.


4.2  Food and non-food, and the semantics of disgust

Categorization of food has a further dimension that makes it unlike the categorization of
many other objects. Rozin and colleagues documented that the distinction between food and
non-food is itself culturally constructed and affectively loaded, and that contamination and
disgust attach to items that cross category boundaries (Rozin and Fallon, 1980, 1987). A food
that looks like something inedible, or that contains an element perceived as contaminating,
is rejected even when the child understands that it is safe. This implies that the regulation of
food acceptance is not merely a matter of liking or disliking sensory properties but is also a
matter of the child’s judgment about what kind of thing a given item is.

   The implication for transformation is double-edged. On the one hand, a preparation that
resembles an accepted food on some dimensions may be treated as an instance of the accepted
category and may inherit its acceptance. On the other hand, a preparation that violates category
expectations on a dimension that matters to the child, for example a familiar dish with an
unexpected color, may be treated as contaminated or wrong. Which dimensions matter is an
empirical question, and it varies from child to child.


4.3  Food chaining as a clinical precedent

The idea that foods can be linked by shared properties and that acceptance can be extended
along the links is not new to clinical practice. A technique called food chaining, described
in a clinical guide by Fraker et al. (2007), begins with foods that a child already accepts and
proposes new foods that share sensory characteristics, such as a similar texture or ﬂavor,
moving gradually along dimensions of similarity. The technique is used by feeding therapists,
and its rationale is similar to the one developed here. Its evidence base, however, is limited. A
chart review of children treated with the approach reported favorable outcomes in children
with feeding aversion (Fishbein et al., 2006), but a review of treated cases without a comparison
group cannot separate the effect of the technique from maturation, repeated exposure, or the
other components of treatment. No controlled trials are cited here, and the published guides
do not provide a formal account of what counts as a small step or how dimensions should be
weighted. The framework developed in the next section aims to supply the missing formal
structure and to identify what an adequate test would look like, without claiming that the
clinical technique has already been validated.

5  The Transformational Familiarity Hypothesis


5.1  Preparations as vectors of properties

To make the notion of similarity among foods precise, let a food preparation be represented as
a vector of properties,

where f denotes ﬂavor, t texture, a aroma, v visual presentation, and c contextual familiarity,
meaning the setting, utensils, serving form, and social circumstances in which the preparation
is encountered. Each component takes values in a space appropriate to it. Flavor, texture, and
aroma may be described by categorical or ordinal descriptors, visual presentation by features
such as shape and color, and context by features such as whether the food is eaten at the usual
table and with the usual implements. No claim is made that these dimensions are exhaustive
or independent. They are a working decomposition, chosen because caregivers commonly
report that children react to each of them separately.

   Let X denote the space of such preparations. At a given time, a child has an accepted set
S ⊂X , consisting of preparations that the child will eat without hesitation, and an unaccepted
region, consisting of preparations that the child refuses. Between them lies a boundary region of
preparations that the child will explore under favorable conditions. The goal of an introduction
is to expand S to include a target preparation z that the child currently refuses and that the
adult wishes to make available, usually for nutritional or cultural reasons.

child with strong textural sensitivity has a large wt, and a child whose acceptance is largely
governed by familiar settings has a large wc. The weights are not assumed to be constant
across foods or over time, and in the present formulation they are unknown quantities to be
estimated from the child’s behavior, not parameters supplied by the theory.


5.2  Chains and the hypothesis

Deﬁnition 1 (Candidate chain). A candidate chain from an accepted preparation x0 ∈S to a target z
is a ﬁnite sequence x0, x1, . . . , xn = z of distinct preparations such that (i) each consecutive pair is close
under dw, that is, dw(xi−1, xi) ≤ϵ for some tolerance ϵ; and (ii) each preparation is safe, nutritionally
acceptable, and offered openly as a variant of the preceding one.

   Conditions (i) and (ii) are geometric and procedural. They do not guarantee that the child
will accept any stage of the chain, still less its endpoint. A candidate chain is therefore a
proposal about a path, and not a claim that the path works.


                                        11

Deﬁnition 2 (Monotone chain). A candidate chain is monotone if the distance to the target never
increases along it, that is, dw(xi, z) ≤dw(xi−1, z) for every i.

   Monotonicity is a property of a restricted class of chains and not a requirement of the theory.
It is a natural ﬁrst model, since it excludes chains that wander, but it also excludes potentially
useful detours. A child might need to become familiar with a new sauce on an otherwise
familiar food before meeting the intended combination, and that intermediate preparation
could lie farther from the target under the chosen distance while creating a more effective route
toward acceptance. Geometric progress toward the target and psychological progress toward
acceptance need not coincide, and whether monotone chains outperform nonmonotone ones
is an empirical question that a later study could address.

   To state what working means, the theory needs an object that depends on the child’s history
and not on the preparation alone.

   Let Yj indicate whether the child voluntarily performs approach behavior j (touching,
smelling, tasting, swallowing, or requesting the food) toward a presented preparation in a

The central object of the theory is a function of three arguments. Two identical preparations
can elicit different responses because they were reached through different histories, and a
theory that attended only to the preparation would miss exactly the effect at issue.

   Because the propensity is latent, it cannot be observed directly, and an estimate of it from
a few encounters is noisy. Success is therefore deﬁned by an empirical criterion, and the

Deﬁnition 3 (Successful chain). Fix in advance a criterion in the form of a number k of voluntary

   Meeting the criterion is an observed event. It is evidence about Aj and is not identical to
it. Keeping the two apart avoids a circularity in which chains are called successful because
an estimated propensity is high and are then used to conﬁrm a theory about that propensity.
Progress is deﬁned by changes in observed behavior and not by geometric proximity alone. A
candidate chain that stalls at stage i has not been refuted as a geometric object. It has supplied
information about the weights w, or about the dimension along which the step was too large.

   The ﬁnal clause of the candidate-chain deﬁnition is substantive. The chain is a sequence of
transparent variations, and the child is not deceived about what is being offered. Concealing
a target food inside an accepted one may produce immediate consumption, but it does not
alter the child’s categories, and it risks the loss of trust when the concealment is discovered.

   The hypothesis can now be stated.

Hypothesis 1 (Transformational Familiarity). Under conditions that are safe, voluntary, and free
of pressure, and in which the child controls the pace and extent of participation, a target z, which is

when it is reached by a candidate chain from an accepted preparation than when it is presented directly,
holding constant the number of offers of the target food, the degree of adult modeling, time with the

is directional and comparative, and it stands or falls on the sign of the difference.  It is a
hypothesis about the effect of the history and not about the preparation, since z is the same
in both cases and only the path by which it was reached differs. The distinction between a
candidate chain and a successful chain matters here, because the hypothesis concerns candidate
chains in general. A study that evaluated only chains that happened to succeed would be
selecting on the outcome.

   Two reﬁnements deserve separate statement.

Hypothesis 2 (Participation). Among children receiving the same chain, those who participate in the
construction of the transformations are more likely to explore the target than those who receive the same
preparations ready-made.

Hypothesis 3 (Dimension speciﬁcity). The tolerance ϵ that supports progress along a chain varies
by dimension, and for some children and some dimensions, ﬁner steps do not improve acceptance and
may reduce it.

   The third hypothesis guards against an assumption that is natural but unsupported, namely
that smaller changes are always better. A child with strong sensory sensitivity may detect
minute variations in texture, and a sequence of nearly identical but not quite identical prepara-
tions may be experienced as an unreliable series of near-misses and not as a gentle progression.
In such a case the optimal strategy may be fewer, larger steps along some dimensions with
strict constancy along others. The theory therefore does not specify a universal step size.
It speciﬁes a search problem in which the adult seeks, through observation of the child’s
responses, a path that holds ﬁxed the properties the child cares most about while varying the
properties the child tolerates varying.

  A reasonable question is what the formalism adds to the ordinary-language statement
that unfamiliar foods should be introduced gradually and openly. By itself, the notation is
a way of stating a search problem, since the weights and the tolerance are not ﬁxed by the
theory. Its payoff is that it makes available claims the ordinary statement does not: that the
dimensions of variation are separable, that children differ in their weights over them, and, as
Hypothesis 3 states, that the best step size is therefore speciﬁc to the dimension and to the

child. The most direct test of the formalism is accordingly whether chains tailored to a child’s
estimated weights outperform chains with uniform steps, and the protocol of Section 11 should
be read with that contrast in mind.

  A ﬁnal hypothesis concerns a higher-order effect. A chain changes a child’s encounters
with one target, but it may also change the child’s expectations about variation itself. A child
who repeatedly meets familiar foods with small, openly explained changes might learn not
only that a particular unfamiliar ingredient is acceptable but that modiﬁcations of familiar
foods are generally safe to investigate.

Hypothesis 4 (Transfer). Children who have followed a candidate chain toward a target are more
likely than children who received matched direct presentation of that target to voluntarily explore a
novel preparation unrelated to the training target, that is, Aj∗(z′ | hchain, s) > Aj∗(z′ | hdirect, s) for a
transfer preparation z′ that was not part of the chain and does not share its key ingredients.

the child’s expectations about culinary variation, or the child’s conﬁdence in exploring it, and
not only familiarity with particular ingredients. That would be a more distinctive contribution
than any effect on a single target, since exposure to the target alone would not anticipate it.

5.4  Relation to exposure and generalization

The hypothesis does not compete with the exposure literature, and it is important to specify
how the two relate. Exposure effects predict that repeated tasting of z will increase acceptance
of z. The chain hypothesis predicts that, in addition, the route by which z is reached matters,
and that an equal number of exposures to z will be more effective when they are preceded by



                                        15

exposure to neighboring preparations that carry some of the properties of z. The generalization
ﬁnding of Birch et al. (1998) supports the plausibility of this, since it suggests that acceptance
of one food transfers to similar foods. The chain hypothesis converts that observation into a
design principle: it proposes constructing the similar foods deliberately and ordering them by
their distance from what is already accepted.

   The hypothesis also differs from simple exposure in the nature of the counterfactual. In a
pure exposure design, the experimenter presents the same item repeatedly, and any resistance
is overcome through accumulated familiarity. In the chain design, the item itself changes
across presentations, and the aim is not to habituate the child to a ﬁxed target but to bring
the target within the family of accepted foods by changing the family boundary as well as
the child’s response. The two strategies can be combined, and a complete intervention would
presumably include repeated exposure to the ﬁnal preparation once it has been reached.


5.5  Alternative explanations

An honest statement of the hypothesis must list the ways it could be wrong. The ﬁrst alternative
is that the chain works by exposure alone, since each step in the chain exposes the child to the
target’s component ingredients. If so, a design that matched exposure to those ingredients
without the ordering would perform equally well. The second is that the chain works through
social modeling, since adults who construct elaborate chains probably also eat more of the
foods in question and attend more closely to the child. A third is that the beneﬁt is due to the
reduction of pressure, since an adult engaged in making variations is less likely to demand that
the child eat. A fourth is a simple expectation effect: a parent who believes in the method will
notice successes and ignore failures. Each of these is consistent with observed improvements
and would not support the hypothesis. The experimental protocol of Section 11 is organized to
separate them.


6  Observational and Participatory Familiarization


6.1  Approach without ingestion

A central assumption of the chain hypothesis is that the child’s ﬁrst successful interaction
with a new preparation need not be consumption. Looking at, smelling, touching, helping
to prepare, and tasting without swallowing are all forms of approach, and each can serve as
a step toward eventual acceptance. This assumption is consistent with the clinical practice
of feeding therapy, which commonly uses a graded sequence of interactions that begins with
tolerating the presence of a food and ends with eating it. It is also consistent with the demand
that the process be low-pressure, because a request to eat is a request for the most difﬁcult
step, and a child who is asked only to look at or touch a food is not placed in a position where
refusal is the only available response.

   The evidence on this point is, as noted in Section 3, mixed. The ﬁnding of Birch et al.



                                        16

(1987) that looking exposure did not raise taste preferences for foods that were never tasted
stands against any simple claim that visual familiarity is sufﬁcient. The nursery intervention
of Dazeley and Houston-Price (2015), by contrast, found that structured non-taste sensory
exposure increased willingness to taste. A reasonable reconciliation is that passive looking
does little, whereas active, multi-sensory interaction in a playful context does something, and
that the beneﬁt is mediated by the reduction of anxiety about the object and not by learning
about its taste. The reconciliation is a conjecture, though it makes a testable prediction: the
beneﬁts of non-taste exposure should be larger for children with higher baseline neophobia
and should be accompanied by changes in approach behavior that precede changes in tasting.

   Approach behaviors can be deﬁned for measurement, with the caveat that they need
not form a single ladder. Candidates are tolerating the food’s presence at the table, looking
at it, touching it with a utensil or hand, smelling it, touching it to the lips, tasting without
swallowing, swallowing a small amount, and eating a portion. Clinical practice often orders
these from least to most demanding, but the ordering is an assumption. A child may smell
a food and refuse to touch it, or taste it without wanting to handle it. Each behavior should
therefore be recorded separately, as Section 11 speciﬁes, and the ordering treated as an empirical
question. Separate recording still allows progress to be detected in children who have not
yet eaten the food. This matters because outcomes conﬁned to intake are insensitive to early
change, and a study that measures only whether the child ate the food will classify as failures
cases in which the child advanced in other ways.


6.2  Modeling as a participatory structure

The social modeling literature supports the use of a trusted adult who eats the target food
in the child’s presence. The way modeling is embedded in the interaction matters. When an
adult eats a food as part of ordinary activity, the child receives information about the food’s
safety with no demand attached. The preschool experiments of Hendy and Raudenbush
(2000) suggest that such modeling is more effective when it is enthusiastic than when it is
silent, so demonstration should not be read as the absence of expression. When the adult
eats while urging the child to do likewise, the information is accompanied by pressure, and
the effect may be reversed. A relevant distinction is between modeling as demonstration,
which may be warm and expressive, and modeling as persuasion, which is to say between
communicating positive engagement and demanding compliance. The former is compatible
with the responsive-feeding framework (Black and Aboud, 2011) and the latter is not.

   Modeling has a further role in the chain framework. Because an adult who is making
intermediate preparations is also eating them, the adult serves as a model for each step, and
the child sees the same person eating a sequence of related foods, each of which is a variation
of the last. This provides evidence, accessible to the child, that the variations belong to a single
family and are safe within it. The point is again conjectural, but it is consistent with the ﬁnding
that children are more willing to eat foods that they have seen a familiar person eat.

7  Procedural and Causal Familiarity: Cultivation and Preparation


7.1  Three kinds of familiarity

The discussion so far has treated familiarity as a matter of the sensory properties of a ﬁnished
food. This is too narrow. A child may become familiar with a food in at least three distinct
ways, and each makes a different contribution.

   Sensory familiarity arises from direct experience of a food’s appearance, smell, texture, and
taste. It is the kind of familiarity that the exposure literature measures, and it develops through
repeated encounters with the food.

    Procedural familiarity arises from knowledge of how a food is obtained and prepared,
including where it comes from, what is done to it, and what role the child’s own actions play
in the process. A child who has planted seeds, watered the plants, harvested the crop, washed
and peeled the produce, and helped prepare it has a history with the food that extends well
beyond the plate.

   Causal familiarity arises from understanding the relation between a raw material and a
ﬁnished dish. A child who mixes ﬂour, water, and yeast, observes the dough rise, and sees
the loaf come from the oven learns that bread is the outcome of a process, and so does not
meet it as an unexplained ﬁnished object. This kind of familiarity makes the transformations
intelligible, and intelligibility is a precondition for a sense of control.

   The three are not independent and need not co-occur. A child can be thoroughly familiar,
sensorially, with a food whose origins are opaque, and a child can be procedurally familiar
with a vegetable that has never been tasted. The point of the distinction is that each type of
familiarity may reduce neophobia by a different mechanism, and that a food environment
which supplies only the ﬁrst has not exhausted the available routes.


7.2  What the evidence shows

Research on gardening and cooking interventions provides suggestive but limited support. A
school-based garden curriculum was associated with improved knowledge of nutrition and
preference for some vegetables in fourth-grade children (Morris and Zidenberg-Cherr, 2002),
and a pre-post study of middle school students reported improved recognition of, attitudes
toward, preferences for, and willingness to taste vegetables (Ratcliffe et al., 2011). A systematic
review of fourteen gardening interventions reported that ten found statistically signiﬁcant
increases in children’s fruit and vegetable consumption, described the evidence as mixed
and limited by convenience samples, small samples, and self-reported intake, judged that
most studies suggest a small positive inﬂuence, and called for controlled and randomized
designs (Savoie-Roskos et al., 2017). On the cooking side, a between-subject experiment with
47 children aged 6 to 10 found that children who helped a parent prepare a lunch ate more
salad, more chicken, and more calories than children whose parent prepared it alone (van der
Horst et al., 2014), a result that is consistent with the participation hypothesis, though the



                                        18

sample was small, the children were older than most of those in the exposure literature, and
the setting was a single meal.

   The limitations of this evidence should be stated plainly. Participation in gardening and
cooking is typically offered by motivated families and schools, so that children who participate
may differ from those who do not. Interventions bundle several components, including
nutrition education, enthusiasm of the adults, and the sheer fact of attention, and the studies
do not isolate which component produces the effect. The question of whether participation
changes acceptance of a food, as distinct from knowledge about it, is therefore open. What
the evidence supports is a weaker claim. Several studies report favorable outcomes, but their
designs do not establish the independent contribution of participation, and the absence of
observed harm in them does not show that such programs are harmless in every setting. Effects
on knowledge and attitudes are also more consistently reported than effects on intake.


7.3 A proposed mechanism

The three-way distinction suggests a mechanism by which participation could matter. A food
that is encountered only as a ﬁnished commodity is, from the child’s perspective, an opaque
object that has arrived from somewhere unknown. Its safety is a matter of faith in the adult
who serves it. A food whose production the child has watched, and in which the child has
participated, is an object whose history is known. The child has seen it as a plant, as a raw
ingredient, and as a result of speciﬁc actions, and has contributed to some of those actions.
Neophobia, understood as caution toward substances whose properties are uncertain, may be
reduced when the uncertainty is reduced by direct knowledge of the substance’s origin and
treatment.

  On this account, participation reduces the novelty of the food in a way that mere tasting
cannot, since it increases the number of channels through which the child has encountered the
food and gives the child a role in producing it. It also increases the child’s sense of authorship
over the food, which may reduce the resistance that arises when food is imposed from outside.
The mechanism would predict that participation matters more for foods that look unfamiliar
in their ﬁnished state, such as whole vegetables with unusual shapes, than for foods that are
already familiar in form.

   This yields a reﬁnement of the participation hypothesis. If participation works by increasing
procedural and causal familiarity, then its effect should depend on the extent to which the child
actually understands the process, and not merely on whether the child was present. A child
who was assigned a trivial task and understood nothing about the larger operation should
beneﬁt less than a child who understood the sequence of transformations. The reﬁnement is
testable, since comprehension can be assessed independently of participation.

7.4  Value beyond acceptance

It would be a mistake to evaluate cultivation and cooking solely by their effects on what
children agree to eat. Growing and preparing food teaches biological processes, measurement,
sequencing, tool use, and practical competence, and it provides opportunities for sustained
collaboration between adults and children. These beneﬁts do not depend on the child’s
developing a taste for any particular vegetable. A program of participation that fails to alter
acceptance of a target food may still be worthwhile on educational grounds, and a conclusion
that treats acceptance as the only criterion of success would undervalue it. This observation is
relevant to the framing of the argument as a whole. If food acceptance is treated as the only
outcome that matters, the pressure to produce it returns by another route, and the conditions
that support exploration are undermined.


8  Structured Environments and the Distribution of Agency


8.1  The division of responsibility

The most inﬂuential practical framework for the relation between caregivers and children at
mealtimes is the division of responsibility proposed by Satter (1986). On this account, the
adult is responsible for what food is offered, when, and where, and the child is responsible for
whether to eat and how much. The framework relies on the assumption that children, given a
suitable environment, are capable of regulating their intake and of broadening their acceptance
over time, and that pressure from the adult interferes with both. Its principles are consistent
with the evidence on pressure and restriction reviewed in Section 3, and with the more general
literature on responsive feeding, which treats feeding as an interaction in which the caregiver
responds contingently to the child’s signals (Black and Aboud, 2011).

   The framework is sometimes misread as permissiveness. It is not permissive about the
adult’s responsibilities, which include the planning, preparation, and presentation of food,
the maintenance of a predictable schedule, and the modeling of eating. What it withholds
from the adult is control over the child’s individual decisions about eating. This is a different
distribution of agency within a structured environment, not an absence of structure. The adult
controls the conditions under which the child decides, and the child controls the decision.


8.2  Autonomy and reactance

Two bodies of psychological theory help to explain why this distribution is effective. The ﬁrst
is self-determination theory, which holds that sustained motivation depends in part on the
satisfaction of a need for autonomy, the experience of acting from one’s own volition (Deci and
Ryan, 2000). A child who eats because of external demands is not experiencing the behavior as
self-directed, and the foods eaten under such conditions may acquire negative associations.
The second is the theory of psychological reactance (Brehm, 1966), according to which people
respond to threats to their freedom by acting to restore it, often by doing the opposite of what


                                        20

is demanded. A demand to eat a food threatens the child’s freedom to refuse, and refusal is
the available means of restoring it. On this view, a fraction of what appears to be picky eating
is reactance, and the appropriate intervention is the removal of the threat.

     It would be a mistake, however, to treat every refusal as an exercise of autonomy. Some
refusals arise from fear, some from sensory distress, and some from fatigue, and attributing
them all to a desire for control is a form of romanticization. The claim of this section is narrower:
whatever the underlying cause of a refusal, the child’s retention of control over the decision
removes one source of resistance, namely the resistance to being controlled, and leaves the
other sources to be addressed by other means.


8.3  Appetite as a facilitating condition

A related question concerns the role of hunger. It is a common saying that hunger improves
the taste of food, and there is a sound physiological basis for the idea that food has greater
motivational value when one is ready to eat. Offering meals at times when children are likely
to have an appetite is therefore sensible, and a snack that spoils appetite shortly before a meal
works against exposure to novel foods.

   The distinction that matters is between appetite as a facilitating condition and hunger
as an instrument of coercion. The ﬁrst consists in arranging the schedule so that the child
arrives at meals with an appetite. The second consists in withholding food, or alternatives
to a refused food, until the child’s hunger is great enough that refusal becomes costly. These
are different practices with different consequences. Deliberate deprivation, intended to make
refusal untenable, is a form of pressure and is subject to the same adverse effects as other forms.
A child who is very hungry is not in a good state for exploration, since distress is incompatible
with the relaxed attention that approach requires. Young children generally do best with
predictable opportunities to eat and the freedom to respond to their own hunger and fullness
cues. The evidence on the direct effect of hunger on acceptance of novel foods is limited,
and the recommendation to schedule meals sensibly rests on the broader responsive-feeding
literature and not on a body of experiments speciﬁc to hunger.

   The same caution applies to adults who manage their own eating by delaying meals until
appetite is high. This may suit some individuals and some circumstances, but it is a personal
pattern and not a general prescription, and its suitability depends on whether it supports
adequate nutrition, energy, and well-being.

9.1  The cost of ﬂexibility

The framework developed so far places demands on the adults who organize the meal. A
household that is to offer intermediate preparations, vary the form of a food across meals,

cook, and to cook with some ﬂuency. If every variation requires a new recipe, a new ingredient
purchase, and a new set of instructions, the cost of ﬂexibility is high, and a rigid menu of a
few accepted dishes is the economical alternative. Households with limited time, equipment,
or money may accordingly ﬁnd it harder to maintain a varied repertoire, and it is plausible
that this affects the range of foods their children are offered. Whether it also affects how often
such children are described as picky is an empirical question on which this essay has no direct
evidence.

inexpensive ingredient into several preparations, adjust the seasoning of a basic product to

same inventory than a cook who can only reheat.

isons between households are meaningful only at the same resolution. Optionality increases
with the size of the inventory, but it also increases with skill and with the breadth of the
acceptable set. Two households with identical inventories may differ greatly in optionality, be-
cause one can produce many acceptable meals from the ingredients and the other can produce
only a few. Cooking competence expands the producibility condition without any change in
expenditure.

   Optionality has a direct application to picky eating. A household with high optionality
can respond to a child’s refusal by offering another preparation of the same nutritious ingredi-
ents, without needing to substitute different foods or to insist on the original. The response
preserves the nutritional objective, preserves the child’s opportunity to explore, and avoids
the confrontation that arises when a single preparation is the only option. The limitation of a


                                        22

low-optionality household is not that its children are more difﬁcult but that its structure leaves
fewer ways to adapt to difﬁculty.


9.3  The continuity of ingredients and the variability of meals

A useful distinction is between repetition of ingredients and repetition of meals. A household
can eat the same staple foods repeatedly without eating the same meal twice. Cooked rice
may become fried rice on one day, a soup on another, and a stufﬁng on a third. A batch of
beans may become a dip, a ﬁlling, a sauce, or a component of another dish. In each case there
is material continuity, in that the same underlying ingredient is carried forward, and sensory
discontinuity, in that the ﬁnished dish differs in ﬂavor, texture, and appearance. The same
noodles can participate in an Italian-style dish, a Southeast Asian-style stir-fry, and a curry
without retaining the identity of the original.

   This pattern bears on the theory in two ways. First, it shows that the identity of a dish is
determined less by its ingredients taken individually than by the relations among them and
the method of preparation, a point that parallels the family-resemblance account of categories.
A child who rejects a vegetable in one dish may accept it in another, not because an aversion
has been overcome but because the overall experience differs. Second, it provides a natural
mechanism for chain construction. Yesterday’s preparation is the starting material for today’s,
and the chain across days is partly a by-product of the way the household uses its inventory
and not a program that must be separately designed.

    Formally, let It be the inventory at the start of day t, a vector of quantities of each ingredient
and prepared item. During the day the household makes purchases Pt, selects a collection of
items Xt to be cooked, and converts them into prepared items Φt(Xt). The conversion map Φt
records the change of identity that cooking effects, and it also absorbs losses such as trimming
and evaporation, so that quantities are conserved only up to those losses. Let Et be the quantity
eaten and Wt the quantity discarded or otherwise lost. The inventory then evolves as

                               It+1 = It + Pt −Xt + Φt(Xt) −Et −Wt,                            (5)

where each term is a vector indexed by item. Cooking therefore changes what the household
possesses and not only how much of it: the inputs Xt leave the inventory and the prepared
items Φt(Xt) enter it. Prepared leftovers are entries of I that are created in this way, and they
carry their own identity, preparation state, and remaining safe storage life, which are tracked
as attributes of the entry. A household that treats these entries as inputs to the next day’s
cooking, and not as waste, has a sequence of meals that is coupled through the inventory. The
coupling reduces waste and cost, and it also produces a series of related preparations, which is
the raw material of a transformation chain. The same representation lets culinary optionality
be deﬁned over a changing inventory, so that Oρ(It, τ, K) varies from day to day as ingredients
are transformed and consumed.

   The storage-life attribute deserves separate emphasis, because it is what limits the length
of a chain built from leftovers. Let σi denote the remaining safe storage life of entry i in


                                        23

the inventory. A step in a chain that draws on an earlier preparation must be taken while
σi remains positive, so a chain that depends on a single batch has a length bounded by the
safe storage life of that batch divided by the interval between steps. Freezing portions at the
outset extends the bound, at the cost of a change in texture that must itself be treated as a
variation along the texture dimension. The constraint does not apply to chains whose steps
are each cooked from fresh components, and the choice between the two is a trade-off among
waste, cost, and ﬂexibility. Public health guidance on safe storage periods governs the limits in
practice, and no particular period is asserted here.

   Optionality also enters the construction of chains directly. A candidate chain is a sequence
of preparations that must each be producible from what the household has, so the number
of candidate chains available from a given inventory grows with Oρ(I, τ, K), and the cost of
constructing a chain falls as optionality rises. The framework therefore predicts that chain-
based interventions will be more feasible in households with higher optionality, and that
optionality moderates the effect of the intervention. Both predictions can be tested by recording
a household-level measure of optionality as a covariate in the protocol of Section 11.

   The practice is subject to a constraint that must not be overlooked. Each transformation
needs to preserve food safety, and repeated reheating does not reset the storage life of a cooked
batch. Public health guidance generally advises that properly refrigerated cooked leftovers
be used within a few days and that portions that will not be used in that time be frozen early.
A strategy that relies on successive transformation of leftovers should be organized around
these limits, and the household that follows it should freeze portions or discard food that has
exceeded its safe storage period, not extend the sequence indeﬁnitely.


9.4  Improvisation and variety

There is also a motivational dimension. Some cooks derive satisfaction from the process of
solving a small, changing problem with whatever materials are at hand, and for them the
changing inventory is a source of interest and not a burden. The preference for variety that this
implies can be economically useful, since it favors ﬂexible use of ingredients over ﬁxed menus
and so tends to reduce waste. A planning strategy in which the day’s meal is determined
jointly by the remaining shelf life of ingredients, the available time, and the preferences of
the moment is the opposite of a rigid weekly plan, and its feasibility depends entirely on the
cook’s ability to improvise.

   The household’s decision problem can be expressed as the maximization, over a sequence
of meals, of a weighted combination of enjoyment, variety, and nutritional adequacy, less
waste and cost, subject to constraints on ingredients, time, equipment, and food safety. No
claim is made that households actually solve such a problem or that the weights are stable.
The formulation serves to display the structure of the trade-offs and to show that skill enters
as a relaxation of constraints, and that variety and low cost are compatible given sufﬁcient
competence. It also shows why a household without that competence faces a harsher trade-off,
in which variety can be bought only by spending more.



                                        24

9.5  Distributional limits

These points must be qualiﬁed by recognition of the constraints that bound them. Time, equip-
ment, food security, disability, and caregiver workload restrict how much experimentation a
household can undertake. A caregiver working several jobs, or caring for several children,
or lacking a functioning kitchen, cannot be expected to construct transformation chains. A
strategy that presumes abundant time and skill, and then attributes the picky eating of children
in resource-constrained households to a failure of method, would both mischaracterize the
situation and add to the burdens that already exist. The argument of this section is that ﬂexibil-
ity is valuable and that skill provides it at low cost. It is not that every household should be
able to supply it. Any intervention based on the framework should therefore be designed with
the constraints of the intended population in mind, and the research agenda should include
simple versions of the strategies that require little time or equipment.


10  Limits, Risks, and Misreadings


The argument of this essay is open to several misreadings that should be addressed directly.

   The ﬁrst is the inference that all food refusal is a solvable problem of presentation. It is
not. Some children have persistent sensory, medical, or developmental feeding difﬁculties that
require specialized assessment and support, and for these children a technique that works for
ordinary neophobia may be ineffective or distressing. The framework offered here applies
to the broad range of ordinary variation, and it comes with a recommendation that children
who show weight loss, nutritional deﬁciency, severe restriction, distress at meals, or feeding
difﬁculty that persists or worsens should be assessed by a clinician. It is also a reason for
caution in using the chain approach with children whose sensory proﬁle is unusual, since the
preservation of ﬁne sensory properties that such children require may leave little room for
variation.

   The second is the opposite inference, that every refusal expresses autonomy and must be
respected as such. Section 8 argued that the retention of control by the child removes one
source of resistance. It did not argue that the child’s preferences are always correct or that
adults have no role in setting the range of foods offered. The adult’s responsibility for offering
a nutritious and varied set of foods is retained.

   The third misreading is that the transformation approach is a method of concealment. As
speciﬁed in Section 5, the chain is a sequence of open variations, and the child is aware of what
is offered. The distinction is both ethical and practical, since concealed foods do not alter the
child’s categories and may damage trust.

   The fourth concerns safety. Allergies, choking hazards, and dietary requirements are not
matters on which experimentation is appropriate, and the introduction of new foods must
respect them. The framework applies to foods that are safe for the child, and the term voluntary
exploration presupposes that the options offered are safe to explore.

   The ﬁfth concerns culture. The foods that a child is expected to accept, and the age at


                                        25

which acceptance is expected, differ across communities, and the notion of a picky eater is
itself culturally situated. A framework that treats a narrow repertoire as a deﬁciency risks
imposing the norms of one culinary tradition on another. Building chains from the household’s
own cuisine makes the construction of a chain culturally neutral in principle, but the choice of
which foods to expand toward is not neutral, and it is made by the adults and the community,
not by the framework. Which foods count as targets is therefore an input to the theory, and the
argument has no implication that any particular foods should be preferred.

   Scope is a further limitation. The essay concerns children, but category structure, procedural
familiarity, and autonomy plausibly operate in adults as well, and food neophobia in adults is
well documented (Pliner and Hobden, 1992). The extension is a natural one, with the difference
that adults can describe their own categories and consent to graded exposure, but it is not
argued here.

    Finally, there is the problem of attribution. Improvements in a child’s acceptance of foods
that follow the introduction of a new strategy are likely to be attributed to the strategy, though
most children’s repertoires broaden with age regardless. Without comparison conditions,
the improvements cannot be assigned to the intervention, and the fact that the experience
of caregivers is dominated by cases that did improve means that the method that was tried
last will often receive the credit. This is the principal reason for insisting on the experimental
design that follows.


11 A Proposed Experimental Protocol


The hypotheses of Section 5 are testable, and this section outlines a design suited to the task.
The design is a proposal, and its parameters would be reﬁned in a pilot study before a full trial.


11.1  Design

The recommended design is a randomized comparison in a setting where meals are served
regularly under a degree of experimental control, such as early-childhood education centers,
with randomization at the level of the child or, where contamination between children is a
concern, at the level of the classroom or center. Children are recruited with parental consent,
with additional consent procedures appropriate to the setting, and children with diagnosed
feeding disorders, relevant allergies, or medical dietary restrictions are excluded from the
experimental conditions and referred to appropriate services. The protocol and analysis plan
should be registered before data collection.

   For each child, one or more target foods are selected from foods that the child currently
refuses, as established in a baseline period by repeated offers without pressure. Selecting
targets individually ensures that the test concerns foods that are actually unaccepted, and the
use of several targets per child, analyzed with appropriate random effects, allows variation
among foods to be modeled.



                                        26

11.2  Conditions

The conditions are arranged so that the number and schedule of offers, adult modeling, time
with the adult, and the child’s motor and social engagement are matched as closely as possible
across arms. Each child attends the same number of sessions of the same duration, the number
of offers of each preparation is ﬁxed in the protocol, and total adult attention is equalized
by providing an attention-matched activity wherever a condition lacks a component. The
matched activity is a non-food activity, such as handling modeling clay or tending a non-edible
plant, supervised by the same adult with the same degree of social engagement. Because a
ﬁxed number of offers does not guarantee equal exposure, the number of tastes taken, the
time the target food is within reach, and the amount of adult talk about the food are recorded
and examined as mediators. Adult modeling is standardized in manner, with a script that
is expressive but contains no invitation or pressure to eat, because the manner of modeling
affects its effectiveness. Standardizing the script ﬁxes its content but not its delivery, so the
delivery is also measured. Sessions are recorded, and raters blind to condition code the adult’s
expressed enthusiasm, vocal and facial affect, eye contact with the child, and any invitation or
pressure to eat. Enthusiasm may act through several routes, including attention, emotional
arousal, perceived social approval, or the informational value of watching another person eat,
and the coded measures allow the contribution of delivery to be examined as a moderator or
mediator without assuming which route operates.

  1. Direct presentation. The target food is offered repeatedly in its standard form, with
    adult modeling and no pressure, together with the attention-matched activity. This is the
    standard exposure condition.

  2. Ordered chain, passive. The child receives a sequence of ready-made preparations along
    a candidate chain from an accepted food to the target, in order, with the same number of
     offers and the same adult modeling as in condition 1. The attention-matched activity ﬁlls
    the time that preparation would otherwise occupy.

  3. Randomized-order chain, passive. The child receives the same set of intermediate
    preparations as in condition 2, with the same number of offers, but in randomized order.

  4. Ordered chain, participatory. The child helps to make the same sequence of preparations
    as in condition 2, so that the ﬁnished foods are equivalent and only the experience of
    construction differs. Children in this condition also receive the matched non-food plant
     activity.

  5. Ordered chain, participatory, with cultivation. As in condition 4, with the addition
     that the child participates in growing or handling the raw ingredient of the target food,
    independently of the preparations, in place of the matched plant activity.

  6. Ingredient-matched control. The child receives the same number of offers of the target’s
    component ingredients in unrelated preparations that do not form a chain.

   Comparison of conditions 1 and 2 tests the central hypothesis, with attention and schedule
matched. Comparison of 2 and 3 tests whether the order of the intermediate preparations


                                        27

matters, apart from exposure to the same set of preparations. Comparison of 2 and 6 tests
whether the similarity structure of the intermediate preparations matters, apart from exposure
to the target’s ingredients, which addresses the ﬁrst of the alternative explanations of Section 5.5.
Comparison of 2 and 4 tests the participation hypothesis, with the passive group receiving the
matched activity so that motor activity, social engagement, and adult attention are equalized
across the two arms. Comparison of 4 and 5 tests the incremental contribution of cultivation.
A six-arm design is demanding, and the contrasts differ in priority. The comparisons of
conditions 1 with 2 and of 2 with 6 are essential, since they test the central hypothesis and
separate it from exposure to the ingredients alone, and the comparison of 2 with 3 is nearly
essential, since it tests whether order matters. The participation contrasts (2 with 4, and 4
with 5) address a separate hypothesis and could be run as a second study, once the ﬁrst has
established whether chains work at all. A further contrast worth reserving for later is between
chains tailored to a child’s estimated weights and chains with uniform steps, which is the most
direct test of the dimension-speciﬁcity hypothesis. Matching reduces confounding but does
not eliminate it, since an attention-matched activity cannot be guaranteed to draw the same
attention as the activity it replaces. The design also does not by itself separate the effect of
modeling from the effect of reduced pressure, and for that purpose the adult’s behavior should
be recorded and rated by observers blind to condition wherever possible.


11.3  Outcomes

Outcomes are recorded separately and are not collapsed into a single scale, because the
behaviors that mark approach need not form a universal hierarchy. A child may smell a
food and refuse to touch it, or taste it without wanting to handle it. For each offer, the
following are recorded as separate binary indicators or frequencies: touching, smelling, mouth
contact or tasting, swallowing, and spontaneous requests for or questions about the food. The
conﬁrmatory outcome is voluntary tasting per offer, because it is the behavior most directly
tied to the hypotheses and is unambiguous to code. The remaining behaviors are secondary
outcomes, each analyzed with mixed-effects models for binary or count data, with random
effects for child, food, and site, and with adjustment for multiplicity speciﬁed in the registered
plan. A composite ordinal approach scale is retained as an exploratory outcome only, and
its use is conditional on evidence from scaling analyses of the pilot data that the behaviors
are in fact ordered in a consistent way. Three further outcomes are kept distinct because they
are related but not interchangeable: liking, measured with an age-appropriate hedonic rating;
willingness to taste, measured by behavior when the food is offered; and intake, measured in
a standard serving. Parent-reported acceptance at home is a further secondary outcome. A
follow-up measurement, taken after the intervention has ended, is needed to assess durability,
since a gain that disappears when the experimental conditions are withdrawn would be of
limited practical value. A chain is regarded as having reached its endpoint when the child
shows stable voluntary exploration of the target across a number of consecutive offers speciﬁed
in the registered plan, and acceptance in the sense of regular eating is analyzed as a separate,
later outcome.



                                        28

A transfer task tests Hypothesis 4. After the intervention, each child is offered a novel
preparation that is unrelated to the training target and does not share its key ingredients,
presented openly as a variation of a different accepted food. The same behaviors are recorded,
and voluntary exploration of the transfer preparation is compared across conditions. A
difference between the chain conditions and the direct and ingredient-matched conditions
would support the transfer hypothesis. An absence of difference would leave any ﬁrst-order
effect on the training target as the only candidate result.


11.4  Covariates and moderators

Baseline neophobia, measured with established child measures (Pliner, 1994), age, sensory
sensitivity, the child’s baseline repertoire, and a household-level measure of culinary optionality
should be recorded. The theory predicts that effects will be moderated by these variables.
In particular, dimension speciﬁcity (Hypothesis 3) predicts that the optimal chain differs by
sensory proﬁle, and the participation reﬁnement of Section 7 predicts that comprehension of
the process moderates the effect of participation. Comprehension can be assessed by asking
children to describe or sequence the steps they have performed.


11.5  Analysis and interpretation

The sample size should be determined by a power analysis based on pilot estimates of between-
condition differences and variance components, and no sample size is asserted here. Analysis
should follow the registered plan, with intention-to-treat as the primary approach. The
interpretation should be proportionate to the results. A result in which condition 2 exceeds
condition 1 but does not exceed condition 6 would be consistent with an explanation in terms
of exposure to the ingredients, without establishing it, and the comparison of conditions 2 and
3 is the cleaner test of whether the order of the transformations matters. A result in which
no condition exceeds the standard exposure control would count against the hypothesis. The
hypothesis is intended to be refutable, and a protocol that could not produce a negative result
would not be a test.


11.6  Ethical considerations

The study involves young children and food, and the standard protections apply, including
parental consent, the child’s ongoing assent as manifested in willingness to participate, the
absence of pressure, and the freedom to decline any step without consequence. Foods are
screened for allergens and choking risk. Because the protocol rests on the claim that coercion is
counterproductive, any element of the design that created pressure to eat would contradict its
premises, and staff should be trained accordingly.
