12  Conclusion


The argument of this essay has been that the question of how to make a child eat is badly posed.
It treats the child as the site of the problem and the food as ﬁxed, whereas the evidence points
to a system in which the form of the food, the way it is introduced, the state of the child, and the
structure of the household all contribute. A refusal conveys information about the interaction
among these elements, and its interpretation depends on which of several mechanisms is
operating. Where the mechanism is neophobia, repeated low-pressure contact is supported by
a substantial literature. Where the mechanism is sensory aversion, accommodation is required.
Where the mechanism is resistance to coercion, the remedy is the removal of pressure. Where
the mechanism is a clinical feeding disorder, specialist care is needed.

   The contribution can be stated compactly. The repeated-exposure model changes the eater’s
response to a ﬁxed food. The proposal developed here changes the pathway by which the
eater encounters the food, and treats the history of encounters, and not the food alone, as
what determines the response. The ﬁrst is well supported. The second is a conjecture that
the protocol above is designed to test. A higher-order version of the conjecture, stated as
the transfer hypothesis, holds that experience with chains may change expectations about
variation itself, and it is tested by a transfer task. A related reﬁnement concerns the endpoint of
a chain. A chain need not terminate in consumption. It may terminate in a stable willingness
to explore the target, with acceptance in the sense of regular eating treated as a separate
and later outcome. Deﬁning success in this way is consistent with the commitment to the
child’s control over participation, and it avoids classifying every attempt that stops short
of eating as a failed intervention. Beyond the established ﬁndings, the essay proposed that
acceptance can be extended by building intermediate preparations that connect accepted and
unaccepted foods, and that participation in the production of these preparations, and in the
cultivation of their ingredients, may contribute procedural and causal familiarity in addition
to the sensory familiarity that exposure supplies. This is the Transformational Familiarity
Hypothesis, together with its participation and dimension-speciﬁcity reﬁnements. These are
conjectures. They draw plausibility from the generalization of acceptance among similar foods,
from the structure of food categories, and from the clinical practice of food chaining, and they
are untested in the form stated here. The protocol of Section 11 speciﬁes how they could be
tested and what results would count against them.

   The argument also relocates part of the problem. If food acceptance depends on the ﬂexibil-
ity of the surrounding environment as well as on the ﬂexibility of the eater, then households
with greater culinary optionality, achieved through skill and not through expenditure, are
better placed to support exploration, and households that lack the time or resources to develop
it face a structural disadvantage that is easily mistaken for a feature of their children. The
practical implication is that support for families should include the means of cooking ﬂexibly,
and that the evaluation of any strategy should consider what it requires of caregivers.

   There is a last point that concerns the aim of the exercise. The value of involving children
in the growing and making of food cannot be measured entirely by what they afterward
agree to eat. A child who learns how a vegetable grows, how dough rises, and how a leftover


                                        30

can become a new dish has acquired understanding and competence that are worth having
whether or not the vegetable becomes a favorite. If acceptance follows, it is a beneﬁt. If it does
not, the child has still gained something, and the conditions that make exploration possible,
which are safety, control, and intelligibility, have been preserved. A framework that keeps
those conditions in view is more likely to produce children who are willing to explore than
one that treats each meal as a contest.
